title: Why Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI need their own AI detection tools
content:
I'm not naive enough to think that these companies don't already have some internal detection tools, but they clearly are not being used enough. Lately researching anything using agents has been a pain (especially if the query leads up to buying intent) - the sources quoted are often AI slop, which are then used to deterministically argue a point. On the first challenge to logic, the reply is usually an apology followed by a tangential search and agreement on the user argued point - sometimes even a hedge. There is a simple problem embedded at the center of this, that at least partially explains this degradation - AI generated text. There is now arguably more AI generated text on the web than human writings, and platforms that used to be very credible (attracting high quality technical writers) now seem to be full of AI generated slop (someone has to call them out). It's a pattern I'm sure most people are noticing under the hood - query -> beautiful prose -> suspect sources. You challenge the answer, and all of a sudden it's a wildly different conclusion. To me that just sounds unreliable, because you could potentially argue with it to generate any conclusion you want - doesn't sound like a reliable brainstorming partner anymore. Not to mention it's preference for believing structured AI prose output as high quality writing. Perhaps it is simply a byproduct of the baked in agreeability or "dooms-day" protections baked in to system prompts. This makes it even more important to have sources quoted by bots verified for authority and origin. The authority test is being easily faked by rampant SEO abuse on once reliable blogging platforms (I won't name them but you know who) - apparently one bot - sorry user - singing product praises is enough for chat to recommend that product, mind-boggling. And one biased - sorry tailored - article comparing a product to 5 competitors is enough to determine which is best. If this is not a crisis, idk what is.
The detection problem: Using conventional techniques like duplicate detection, repetition and similarity filters on AI generated content is a lost cause - there's enough probabilistic variance in them to generate millions of different copies.
One solution to the problem: Use an AI detector to adjust result ranks. By adjusting the ranking using AI generated labels, not only will engines prioritise genuine human writings - they also potentially refer to a wider range of opinions on a subject, improving diversity consulted in answers. I know it sounds like an over-simplification, and it probably is - but to me it does sound like a first step in the right direction.
Taken from https://t9xt.com/writings/why-google-microsoft-anthropic-and-openai-need-to-build-their-own-ai-detection-tools-before-it-i

report.summary: With AI slop flooding the web and poisoning agent research, one writer argues Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI must build their own AI detectors to restore trustworthy ranking.
report.background: Since late 2022, generative models have made it cheap to produce unlimited plausible prose, and content farms, affiliate marketers and SEO operators have exploited that at industrial scale. Studies and crawler analyses suggest a large and growing share of newly published web pages is machine-generated. At the same time, assistants have shifted from answering questions to browsing and citing sources, which means their answers now inherit whatever junk ranks well. Detection has been a public failure so far: OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in 2023 over poor accuracy, and academic detectors struggle with paraphrased or lightly edited output. Meanwhile platforms like Google and Microsoft are commercially conflicted, since AI summaries and AI content both feed their ad and licensing businesses. That conflict is exactly what the author is pointing at.
key_points: The web is now saturated with machine-written text, including on platforms that once attracted high-quality technical writers. The author argues the volume of AI prose arguably exceeds human writing, so any research workflow that trusts the open web is now pulling from a contaminated corpus.

Agent-based research feels unreliable because of sycophancy. Challenge a cited answer and the model apologizes, silently swaps sources and agrees with you instead. The author notes you can argue your way to nearly any conclusion, which makes these tools useless as brainstorm partners or fact-checkers.

Authority signals are trivially faked. A single bot-written product rave, or one 'tailored' comparison article against five competitors, is apparently enough to make a chatbot recommend a product. Rampant SEO abuse on formerly credible blogging platforms has broken the trust heuristics models rely on.

Conventional detection is a dead end. Duplicate checks, repetition filters and similarity matching fail because probabilistic variance lets a model generate millions of near-unique variants of the same claim, defeating fingerprint-style approaches.

Proposed fix: treat AI-detection labels as a ranking signal. Downranking likely generated pages could surface genuine human writing and, crucially, widen the range of opinions an assistant consults, improving answer diversity even if detection is imperfect.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes detection from a plagiarism policing tool into core search and retrieval infrastructure, which puts Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic in an awkward position: they would be ranking against their own output. Expect pressure toward provenance standards, detector-integrated retrieval and licensing deals for verified human content. For developers, source verification, domain reputation scoring and detector scores become real components of RAG pipelines rather than afterthoughts, and any agent that cites sources will be judged on citation quality, not prose fluency. For regular users, the near-term effect is continued erosion of trust: answers that look authoritative and collapse under a single follow-up question. The practical advice is to verify primary sources manually and treat confident citations as claims, not evidence.
report.tools: Worth watching: Pangram and GPTZero for commercial detection, plus the open-source Binoculars detector and the RAID benchmark for evaluating robustness. DetectGPT and watermarking research (including Google DeepMind's SynthID) cover the generation side. For provenance, look at C2PA content credentials and emerging web standards for signed origin metadata. On the retrieval side, experiment with domain allowlists, citation-verification steps in your agent loop, and search APIs that expose source quality signals.
